Classification and null guard: both edges assert association only (etiologicalConsensus NOT_ESTABLISHED, vaNexusProbabilityAlignment NOT_ASSERTED, hypothesizedOnly:true), at NEUROLOGICAL_DEGENERATION and INFECTIOUS_SPREAD respectively. Both edges carry the located NULLS on the face of the record rather than omitting them. The rank 1 edge records that the located scoping review found the most common systemic comorbidities in seborrhoeic dermatitis patients to be hypertension and diabetes but NOT statistically significant, and that obesity was common but ALSO not significant, because those are the comorbidities a reviewer is most likely to assume. The rank 2 edge records the clinicopathological study's explicit null that seborrhoeic-like dermatitis severity did NOT significantly correlate with CD4 count, viral load, or antiretroviral therapy, and the scoping review's note that the prevalence of comorbid seborrhoeic dermatitis MAY BE DECREASING as antiretroviral therapy use increases. The rank 1 edge labels its mechanism review as hypothesis-generating on the face of the edge.

Withheld routes and duplicate-scope screen: no psoriasis edge (SCOPE AND IDENTITY-RISK - psoriasis and seborrhoeic dermatitis are a recognised differential of a scaly eruption but the located evidence assembled for this file does not support a psoriasis association, and the registry already carries a direct psoriasis-to-eczema edge while the catalog separately carries both eczema and atopic-dermatitis-eczema as open identities for the same disease, so this batch deliberately adds no edge to either eczema identity and that restraint is recorded here); no fungal-skin-infection edge (MECHANISM-CLASS MISMATCH - seborrhoeic dermatitis is associated with Malassezia, a lipophilic yeast and commensal, whereas the catalog fungal-skin-infection identity is Tinea Pedis / Fungal Infections, a dermatophyte group, and the meta-analysis lists dermatophytosis as a separate condition from seborrhoeic dermatitis, so conflating them would be a category error); no depressive-disorder or other mood edge (DIRECTION REVERSAL - the located scoping review reports that around 16 percent of individuals with psychiatric disorders had seborrhoeic dermatitis, which conditions on the psychiatric condition and therefore runs psychiatric-disease to seborrhoeic dermatitis rather than the reverse, and the registry already carries 90 incoming edges to depressive-disorder from other primaries); and no osteoporosis edge (THIN SUPPORT - the located scoping review reports higher prevalence and faster progression of osteoporosis in individuals with comorbid seborrhoeic dermatitis, but that is a single cited finding within a narrative scoping review with no companion anchor located for it, so it is recorded as a named candidate for a future batch rather than authored on one source).

nexusClaim.associationBasis: Seborrhoeic dermatitis is the most frequently reported skin finding in Parkinson's disease and the association is bidirectional in the located evidence, with a severity gradient running in both directions: a scoping review of systemic comorbidities associated with seborrhoeic dermatitis reports that nearly half of Parkinson's disease patients in one study also had seborrhoeic dermatitis, that as the severity of Parkinson's disease symptoms increases the development of seborrhoeic dermatitis is observed to occur at a much higher rate, and that the burden of seborrhoeic dermatitis is positively correlated to the severity of Parkinson's symptoms, and it explicitly frames the whole comorbidity literature as highlighting the complex nature of seborrhoeic dermatitis and underscoring the necessity of further research (PMID 39669846); a cross-sectional study examining the association of seborrhoeic dermatitis and Parkinson's disease is registered as the dedicated paired-design source for this edge (PMID 39313034); and a narrative review sets out the genetic, lipid, fungal-microbiome, and neuroinflammatory links proposed between the two diseases, which is the located source for the candidate mechanisms rather than for the association itself (PMID 42650087); recorded as documented association only, with the direction recorded as unresolved and with the scoping review's own nulls for the most commonly cited seborrhoeic comorbidities carried openly on the file.
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation is established for any individual, and the located evidence supports association in both directions without resolving which is antecedent: the scoping review frames the finding from the Parkinson's population, reporting how many Parkinson's patients also have seborrhoeic dermatitis and how that prevalence rises with Parkinson's severity, while the file's own identity is the skin disease, so the clinically operative arrow runs Parkinson's to seborrhoeic dermatitis and this edge is the reciprocal view. Whether the association reflects a shared upstream driver, in which alpha-synuclein biology, altered sebum lipid composition, and Malassezia proliferation each plausibly contribute to both, or a genuine consequence of Parkinson motor dysfunction on facial sebaceous function, cannot be separated by the located cross-sectional design, and the review's own proposal of genetic, lipid, fungal-microbiome, and neuroinflammatory links is explicitly a set of hypotheses rather than tested mechanisms. The scoping review also records that in one cross-sectional study of patients with seborrhoeic dermatitis the most common systemic comorbidities were hypertension and diabetes, that this finding was NOT statistically significant, and that obesity was common but ALSO not significant, which is registered as a null here because those are the comorbidities a reviewer is most likely to assume. Individual claims require a dated Parkinson's diagnosis with motor and non-motor staging, a dated seborrhoeic dermatitis diagnosis with distribution documented, and a dated assessment of whether the skin disease predated, postdated, or tracked the neurological staging.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: The hypothesised vector is a shared alpha-synuclein and autonomic-secretion pathway in which the neurodegenerative process alters sebaceous gland function and facial motor control, and in which an altered sebum lipid environment permits Malassezia overgrowth that drives the visible dermatitis, with the located review naming genetic, lipid, fungal-microbiome, and neuroinflammatory links as candidate connections and the located narrative review specifically examining alpha-synuclein effects on the lipid phenotype of human sebocytes in the Parkinson's context; the mechanism is classified NEUROLOGICAL_DEGENERATION to match the existing registry precedent for this target identity, which carries that category on one of its two incoming edges, and the vector is offered as a hypothesis linking two conditions that the located evidence reports as associated and explicitly not as a demonstrated pathway.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: Authored at ASSOCIATION_ONLY at scoping-review, cross-sectional, and narrative-mechanism class, following the file's existing dermatologic, autoimmune, and treatment-related pathway scope: the scoping review is the anchor that supplies both the magnitude, nearly half of Parkinson's patients in one study, and the bidirectional severity gradient, that seborrhoeic dermatitis burden rising with Parkinson's symptom severity (PMID 39669846); the cross-sectional study is the dedicated paired-design source for this exact association (PMID 39313034); and the narrative review is registered for the candidate mechanisms rather than for the association, and is explicitly labelled as hypothesis-generating in the edge (PMID 42650087). Because the direction is unresolved and the mechanisms are proposed rather than tested, the conservative standard holds the edge at association only, records the reciprocal-arrow framing, and carries the scoping review's own non-significant hypertension, diabetes, and obesity findings openly on the file rather than letting a reviewer assume them.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: The scoping review is a Cureus scoping review, not a systematic review with pooled estimates, and its located abstract reports the underlying studies' findings narratively without confidence intervals, so the nearly-half figure is a single cited study's result rather than a pooled prevalence; the cross-sectional study is a single-pair design that cannot establish temporal order and whose located abstract is a short communication without the effect estimate in the retrieved text; the narrative review is by construction a hypothesis paper, and its genetic, lipid, fungal-microbiome, and neuroinflammatory links are proposed connections, not tested ones; the scoping review itself states that these associations underscore the necessity of further research; NO located anchor reports seborrhoeic dermatitis prevalence in a Parkinson's cohort with a non-Parkinson comparison group; and no located anchor reports whether treating the Parkinson's motor symptoms alters the skin disease, which is the question that would distinguish a shared driver from a consequence. The scoping review's non-significant findings for hypertension, diabetes, and obesity are registered as nulls on the file so that the most commonly assumed seborrhoeic comorbidities are not treated as established here.
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: Drug-induced seborrhoeic or sebaceous phenotype, including from dopaminergic agents, levodopa, and other agents affecting sebum composition
Malassezia overgrowth from a different driver such as immunosuppression, including HIV-related and transplant-related immunosuppression
Concurrent atopic dermatitis or psoriasis, which the same scoping review places among the differential of a scaly facial eruption and which belong to different catalog identities

Age-related sebaceous gland change, since both Parkinson's disease and seborrhoeic dermatitis increase in prevalence with age and the located cross-sectional design cannot age-adjust the reported association from the retrieved text

suggestions.rationale: Authoring registers this edge because seborrhoeic dermatitis is the most frequently reported skin finding in Parkinson's disease, because the located scoping review supplies a severity gradient running in both directions rather than a bare co-occurrence, and because the operational reading is a screening proposition: a patient newly diagnosed with Parkinson's should be examined for the skin disease, and a patient with unexplained seborrhoeic dermatitis warrants neurological review. nexusClaim.associationBasis: Seborrhoeic dermatitis is among the commonest dermatological diagnoses in people living with HIV, and the located evidence supplies both a pooled prevalence and a histopathological signature: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 145 articles involving 41,285 people with HIV identified approximately 28,448 patients with dermatological disease, and among 60,064 dermatological events found the most prevalent conditions to be oral candidiasis at 8.88 percent, dermatophytosis, SEBORRHEIC DERMATITIS, warts, and herpes zoster, with an overall prevalence of dermatological disease of 76 percent (95 percent CI 72 to 81) and significant heterogeneity at I squared 97 percent (PMID 41162862); a prospective clinicopathological study of 30 HIV-seropositive adults presenting with seborrhoeic-like dermatitis found 50 percent showed severe or very severe disease and 6 patients (20.0 percent) presented with erythroderma, and confirmed that confluent parakeratosis, necrotic keratinocytes, plasma cells, neutrophils with leukocytoclasia, and leukoexocytosis are histopathological clues to seborrhoeic-like dermatitis occurring in HIV-seropositive patients, so that the presence of these features in a skin biopsy is itself a clue to the diagnosis of HIV (PMID 32379092); and the scoping review of seborrhoeic comorbidities reports that HIV is a disease with higher incidence of seborrhoeic dermatitis, while noting that the prevalence of comorbid seborrhoeic dermatitis MAY BE DECREASING as antiretroviral therapy use increases (PMID 39669846); recorded as documented association only, with the primary anchor's heterogeneity and the located explicit null on severity correlation carried openly.
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation is established for any individual, and the located evidence is genuinely mixed in a way this edge records rather than smooths over: the meta-analysis reports a 76 percent overall prevalence of ANY dermatological disease with I squared 97 percent, so its seborrhoeic-dermatitis contribution is one component of a very heterogeneous literature and must not be read as an individual risk figure; the clinicopathological study explicitly found NO significant correlation between seborrhoeic-like dermatitis severity and CD4 count, viral load, or antiretroviral therapy, which is a direct null on the natural assumption that the skin disease tracks HIV disease activity, and that null is registered on the face of this edge; the scoping review notes the prevalence of comorbid seborrhoeic dermatitis may be DECREASING as antiretroviral therapy increases, which cuts against any assumption of a stable or rising contemporary association; and the histopathological study is 30 patients from a single South African dermatology clinic, so the histological clues are suggestive rather than diagnostic. Individual claims require a dated HIV diagnosis with CD4 count, viral load, and antiretroviral therapy history, a dated seborrhoeic or seborrhoeic-like dermatitis diagnosis with severity documented, and where the biopsy signature is relied upon, dermatopathology review.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: The hypothesised vector is immune dysregulation from HIV infection permitting Malassezia overgrowth in sebaceous areas, so that a common commensal yeast produces a clinically significant inflammatory eruption, with advanced immunosuppression proposed as intensifying the eruption; the vector is named as a permissive-immunity route rather than a direct viral invasion route because the located evidence documents a dysregulated host response to a commensal organism rather than viral involvement of the skin, and the located clinicopathological study's finding that severity did not correlate with CD4 count, viral load, or therapy is carried openly as the principal challenge to the intensity component of that hypothesis.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: Authored at ASSOCIATION_ONLY at systematic-review-and-meta-analysis, prospective-clinicopathological, and scoping-review class, following the file's existing dermatologic, autoimmune, and treatment-related pathway scope: the meta-analysis is the anchor that supplies the pooled dermatological prevalence structure and places seborrhoeic dermatitis among the commonest conditions, and is registered together with its I-squared 97 percent heterogeneity so the pooled figure is not over-read (PMID 41162862); the clinicopathological study is the anchor that supplies the histopathological signature and the explicit null on CD4 count, viral load, and therapy, which is the located justification for holding this edge at association only (PMID 32379092); and the scoping review supplies the contemporary-trend observation that the prevalence of comorbid seborrhoeic dermatitis may be decreasing with antiretroviral therapy (PMID 39669846). Because the primary anchor is heavily heterogeneous and the second reports a direct null on disease-activity correlation, the conservative standard holds the edge at association only, records both limits explicitly, and requires dated HIV status with immunological parameters rather than the skin finding alone.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: The meta-analysis reports 76 percent (95 percent CI 72 to 81) overall prevalence of ANY dermatological disease with I squared 97 percent, which is extreme heterogeneity, and its seborrhoeic-dermatitis component is reported as a ranked position among commonest conditions rather than as a pooled seborrhoeic-specific estimate; its search spanned 1975 to November 2022 across MEDLINE, Web of Science, Google Scholar, and grey literature with JBI risk-of-bias appraisal, and its own stated limitations include small sample sizes, insufficient study-setting descriptions, and difficulties in diagnosing both HIV and dermatological disease; the clinicopathological study is 30 patients (13 women, 17 men) from a single South African dermatology clinic with a 20 percent erythroderma rate, and its central null, that severity did not significantly correlate with CD4 count, viral load, or antiretroviral therapy, is reported as a finding requiring further studies with larger populations; the scoping review explicitly cautions that the prevalence of comorbid seborrhoeic dermatitis may be decreasing as antiretroviral therapy increases, so the association may be attenuating in the contemporary era; NO located anchor reports seborrhoeic dermatitis prevalence in an HIV-negative comparison group drawn from the same populations as the pooled analysis, so the excess attributable to HIV cannot be isolated; and no located anchor reports whether the erythrodermic presentation is more frequent in HIV than in HIV-negative seborrhoeic dermatitis. Erythroderma and the oral candidiasis and dermatophytosis findings in the same meta-analysis were reviewed and are not authored, since oral candidiasis has no catalog identity and dermatophytosis is catalogued as fungal-skin-infection with a different organism class than Malassezia.
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: Antiretroviral therapy as an alternative explanation for changing or atypical skin phenotype, since the located clinicopathological study found no significant correlation with therapy and the scoping review notes prevalence may be falling as therapy use increases
Atopic dermatitis or psoriasis as a coexisting scaly facial eruption belonging to a different catalog identity, which the same differential applies to regardless of HIV status
Drug-induced seborrhoeic or sebaceous phenotype, including from agents taken in the context of HIV treatment
Malassezia overgrowth arising in the absence of HIV, which is the common presentation and therefore the necessary comparator for any HIV-attributed individual claim

evidenceGaps: The meta-analysis reports 76 percent (95 percent CI 72 to 81) overall prevalence of ANY dermatological disease with I squared 97 percent, which is extreme heterogeneity, and its seborrhoeic-dermatitis component is reported as a ranked position among commonest conditions rather than as a pooled seborrhoeic-specific estimate; its search spanned 1975 to November 2022 across MEDLINE, Web of Science, Google Scholar, and grey literature with JBI risk-of-bias appraisal, and its own stated limitations include small sample sizes, insufficient study-setting descriptions, and difficulties in diagnosing both HIV and dermatological disease; the clinicopathological study is 30 patients (13 women, 17 men) from a single South African dermatology clinic with a 20 percent erythroderma rate, and its central null, that severity did not significantly correlate with CD4 count, viral load, or antiretroviral therapy, is reported as a finding requiring further studies with larger populations; the scoping review explicitly cautions that the prevalence of comorbid seborrhoeic dermatitis may be decreasing as antiretroviral therapy increases, so the association may be attenuating in the contemporary era; NO located anchor reports seborrhoeic dermatitis prevalence in an HIV-negative comparison group drawn from the same populations as the pooled analysis, so the excess attributable to HIV cannot be isolated; and no located anchor reports whether the erythrodermic presentation is more frequent in HIV than in HIV-negative seborrhoeic dermatitis. Erythroderma and the oral candidiasis and dermatophytosis findings in the same meta-analysis were reviewed and are not authored, since oral candidiasis has no catalog identity and dermatophytosis is catalogued as fungal-skin-infection with a different organism class than Malassezia.
suggestions.rationale: Authoring registers this edge because seborrhoeic dermatitis is among the commonest dermatological diagnoses in people living with HIV, because the located clinicopathological study supplies a histopathological signature that a dermatopathologist can act on, and because the operational reading is screening: a seborrhoeic-like eruption with the described histological features warrants HIV testing. The conservative framing records the meta-analysis's I-squared 97 percent heterogeneity so the pooled figure is not over-read, carries the study's explicit null on CD4 count, viral load, and therapy, notes the reported contemporary decrease in prevalence with therapy, and requires dated HIV status with immunological parameters rather than the skin finding alone.

Anchors are the PRISMA scoping review of seborrhoeic comorbidities reporting that nearly half of Parkinson's patients in one study also had seborrhoeic dermatitis, that seborrhoeic dermatitis development rose with Parkinson's severity and that its burden correlated positively with Parkinson's severity, and explicitly recording the NON-SIGNIFICANT findings for hypertension, diabetes, and obesity (PMID 39669846); the dedicated cross-sectional seborrheic-dermatitis and Parkinson's association study (PMID 39313034); the narrative review of genetic, lipid, fungal-microbiome, and neuroinflammatory links, registered as hypothesis-generating for mechanism (PMID 42650087); the systematic review and meta-analysis of 145 articles and 41,285 people with HIV finding seborrhoeic dermatitis among the most prevalent dermatological conditions with an overall dermatological prevalence of 76 percent (95 percent CI 72 to 81) and I squared 97 percent heterogeneity (PMID 41162862); the prospective clinicopathological study of 30 HIV-seropositive adults confirming confluent parakeratosis, necrotic keratinocytes, plasma cells, neutrophils with leukocytoclasia, and leukoexocytosis as histological clues, and reporting NO significant correlation between severity and CD4 count, viral load, or therapy (PMID 32379092); and the scoping review's note that the prevalence of comorbid seborrhoeic dermatitis may be decreasing as antiretroviral therapy use increases (PMID 39669846). The mood route is withheld on direction reversal, the fungal route on a Malassezia-versus-dermatophyte class mismatch, and the psoriasis route on scope and eczema identity-duplication risk.
